chapter.title: Your three accounts

cards.body: Your shares aren't kept in your broker's name, so where do they actually live? In the bazaar you need three things: a purse for rupees, a licensed agent who carries your order to the stalls, and **a locker in a guarded vault, in your name**, where your slices are kept. That's your bank account, your trading account and your demat account.
cards.simpler: Your shares aren't kept in your broker's name. So where are they? Picture a busy bazaar. You need three things: a purse for your rupees, a licensed agent who takes your order to the stalls, and **a locker in a guarded vault, in your name**, where your slices are kept. The purse is your bank account. The agent is your trading account. The locker is your demat account.

cards.prompt: Priya buys 2 shares on a Tuesday, paid for from her savings account. By Thursday, where are those 2 shares kept?

options.text: In her savings account, next to her salary
In a demat account in her own name
In her broker's company account, until she sells

whyNot.a: That's the purse, not the locker: a bank account holds rupees, never shares.
whyNot.c: That's the agent, not the vault: the broker places the order, but the shares go into an account in Priya's name.

cards.reteach: Picture the bazaar again. Your purse pays, the agent shops, and whatever he buys goes straight into a locker with your name on it. The bank is the purse, the broker is the agent, the demat account is the locker.

cards.title: Three accounts, three jobs
cards.body:
You need **three accounts, each with one job**. Your bank account holds rupees. It's the same savings account your salary already lands in, so you probably have this one.

Your trading account is opened with a *broker*, a company registered with SEBI to place orders on NSE and BSE for you. Think of the agent at the bazaar gate holding your shopping list. You can't place orders on the exchange yourself.

Your demat account (short for *dematerialised*: shares kept as computer records, not paper certificates) is the locker. Shares go in. Rupees never do.
cards.simpler:
You need **three accounts, each with one job**. Your bank account holds rupees, and it's the savings account your salary already lands in.

Your trading account sits with a broker, a company registered with SEBI. It places orders on NSE and BSE for you, like the agent at the bazaar gate. You can't place them yourself.

Your demat account (short for dematerialised: shares kept as computer records, not paper) is the locker. Shares go in. Rupees never do.

cards.title: Arjun's first ₹2,000
cards.body: Arjun, in Pune, moves ₹2,000 from his bank to his trading account. He buys 1 share priced at ₹1,500. The next working day, **the share appears in his demat account**, and about ₹500 (minus a few rupees of charges) waits in his trading account for his next order. His bank app shows ₹2,000 gone and nothing in return, which is exactly what it should show.
cards.simpler: Arjun lives in Pune. He moves ₹2,000 from his bank to his trading account, then buys 1 share at ₹1,500. The next working day, **the share shows up in his demat account**. About ₹500, minus a few rupees in charges, stays in his trading account for his next order. His bank app shows ₹2,000 gone and nothing back. That looks odd, but it's exactly right.

cards.prompt: Kavya bought 5 shares last year and can't remember if she sold any. Where should she look to see what she owns right now?

whyNot.a: That's the purse, not the locker: the passbook shows rupees moving, not shares held.
whyNot.b: That's the shopping list, not the locker: order history shows what she bought, not what's still hers.

cards.reteach: Each account answers one question. Bank: how many rupees do I have? Trading account: what orders did I place? Demat: what shares do I own today? Kavya is asking the third one.

cards.title: The locker isn't at the broker's
cards.body: You'd think the broker keeps your shares. Usually it just opens the locker for you and holds a key. **The locker sits with a depository**, either NSDL or CDSL, India's two depositories, which record every share in its owner's name. If your broker shuts down, your shares are still recorded in your name, and a new broker can help you move them into a fresh locker of your own.
cards.simpler: Your broker doesn't keep your shares. Usually it just opens the locker for you and holds a key. **The locker sits with a depository**: NSDL or CDSL, India's two, which record every share in its owner's name. If your broker shuts down, your shares are still in your name. A new broker can help you move them into a fresh locker of your own.

cards.body: Meera sells 3 shares for ₹4,500 and checks her bank app the next day. Nothing. She's halfway through an angry message to her broker when she spots it: the money is sitting in her trading account, ready for her to tap withdraw (if she doesn't, brokers send unused cash back to the bank on a regular schedule anyway). Money from a sale lands in the middle account first, so **when cash looks missing, check the trading account before you panic**.

cards.prompt: Your cousin says, "If my broker's app ever shuts down, my shares vanish with it." What's the best reply?

options.text: True, so only ever use the biggest broker
No, they're in your bank account, so they're safe
No, they stay recorded in your name at NSDL or CDSL, and you can move them to a new broker

whyNot.a: That's mixing up the agent and the vault: the broker places orders, and the depository holds the shares.
whyNot.b: That's the purse, not the locker: banks hold rupees, not shares.

cards.reteach: The broker holds a key, not the vault. Your shares are recorded in your name at NSDL or CDSL, whichever broker you use. Lose the key-holder and a new broker helps you move your shares into a fresh locker, still in your name. They never vanish.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Purse pays, agent shops, locker holds: **bank, trading, demat (at NSDL or CDSL)**. Rupees travel from your purse to the agent at the gate, and whatever he buys goes into a locker with your name on it, not the broker's.
cards.simpler: The purse pays, the agent shops, the locker holds. That's **your bank, your trading account and your demat (kept at NSDL or CDSL)**. Rupees go from your bank to your trading account. Your shares land in your demat, in your name, not the broker's.

cards.body:
Tonight, open the income tax e-filing website and **check that your PAN is linked to your Aadhaar**. If it isn't linked, your PAN stops working and KYC (the identity check a broker does) can't go through. Two minutes, no broker needed.

Tomorrow: the one setting that stops you paying more than you meant to.
cards.simpler:
Tonight, go to the income tax e-filing website and **check that your PAN is linked to your Aadhaar**. If they aren't linked, your PAN stops working, and your KYC (the identity check a broker does) can't go through. It takes two minutes, and you don't need a broker for it.

Tomorrow: the one setting that stops you paying more than you meant to.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now name your three accounts and say which one holds your shares and which one holds your cash.

dubious_claims: Meera's sale money 'waiting for her to tap withdraw' is only partly true: under SEBI's running-account settlement, brokers must send unused money back to the bank every month or quarter, so the cash doesn't wait there forever (minor detail, not false).
repairedFrom.why: The 'In one breath' recap has no concrete image, and its 'Tomorrow' teaser sits above an unrelated PAN–Aadhaar card, so the chapter doesn't end on the open loop.
